name: Summarise Group Discussion
instruction: Listen to three speakers. Summarise the topic, each person’s contribution, and how their views relate to one another.
title: Extending library opening hours
narration: Three students are discussing whether the university library should extend its opening hours.
turns: Maya

I think the library should stay open later throughout the semester, not only during exams. Some students work in the evening and need somewhere quiet afterwards. My shared house is noisy, so having access until midnight would make a real difference. What do you both think?
Ben

I understand the need, but opening the whole building could be expensive. We would need security, lighting and staff even if only a few students came. I would rather see a limited late-opening area, with student-card access, than promise a service the library cannot sustain.
Clara

A small area sounds sensible, but getting home safely is another issue. The last bus leaves before midnight. Students without cars might not benefit unless transport is considered too. Perhaps the university could coordinate a shuttle on the busiest nights rather than run it every evening.
Maya

That is a fair point. I do not need the borrowing desk to stay open; I mainly need a desk, power and internet. We could start with the ground-floor study room. A short survey might tell us which nights working students actually need it most.
Ben

I would support a trial based on that survey. We could count visits and check the cost for six weeks, then decide whether to continue. Clear rules would matter, especially about noise, visitors and what students should do if they need help after staff leave.
Clara

Then our recommendation could combine a small supervised study area with a transport check. We should ask students about both demand and travel, and make sure accessibility is included. That gives the university evidence before it commits to opening the entire library later.

Maya supports later opening because work and noisy housing limit study opportunities.
Ben worries about cost and proposes a small card-access area with rules and a six-week trial.
Clara raises safe transport and accessibility, suggesting a shuttle on busy nights.
The group converges on surveying demand and trialling a limited study area alongside transport planning.

Clara adds that safe travel is equally important, since the last bus leaves before midnight, and proposes checking shuttle options and accessibility. Maya accepts the smaller-area idea because she mainly needs a desk and internet, not a borrowing service. The discussion therefore moves from a general request for longer hours towards a more practical proposal: survey students, trial a limited study space and consider transport before expanding the service.

title: Choosing a group-project format
narration: Three students are discussing how to present their environmental group project.
turns: Daniel

For our environmental project, I would like to make a short video instead of a slide presentation. We could show the recycling facilities around campus and interview students. That might make our findings easier to understand than reading statistics from a screen during the final class.
Leah

A video could be engaging, but editing takes time and none of us has much experience. We also have to show how we collected and analysed our data. I worry that production work might distract us from the research, which is the main part of the assessment.
Omar

Could we combine the approaches? A few short clips could introduce the problem, followed by slides explaining the evidence. We should also provide captions and avoid filming anyone without permission. The format should help communicate the findings rather than become the main focus of the project.
Daniel

I like that compromise. We could record the facilities without identifying students, and use an anonymous questionnaire instead of interviews. I can take responsibility for two brief clips. If the clips do not work well, the research presentation would still be complete without them.
Leah

That makes the workload more manageable. Let us agree on the research questions and divide the analysis first. Then we can set a strict time limit for filming and editing. I would also like us to practise together so the final presentation feels like one coherent explanation.
Omar

Agreed. We should check the assessment instructions before committing, share a draft early and keep the clips short and accessible. The final plan is a slide-based presentation supported by video, with research quality, consent and clear teamwork taking priority over elaborate production.

title: Improving campus food choices
narration: Three students are discussing ways to improve food choices in the campus cafeteria.
turns: Aisha

I would like the cafeteria to offer more affordable plant-based meals. There is usually one option, but it is often the same dish. Students with different diets should have a genuine choice, and some of my friends bring lunch because the available meals are too expensive.
Tom

More choice sounds good, but the kitchen already throws away food when demand is low. Adding several dishes every day could make that worse. I think the cafeteria should first find out what students would actually buy and whether it can use ingredients across different meals.
Sophie

Price and information matter too. A meal may look suitable but contain an ingredient someone cannot eat. Clear labels would help. We could ask for one rotating, reasonably priced dish each day and make sure staff can answer questions, instead of expanding the whole menu at once.
Aisha

A rotating dish would be a useful start, especially if students could suggest recipes. I do not expect every meal to suit everyone. I mainly want variety across the week and a price that makes buying lunch realistic for students who are watching their budgets.
Tom

Then we should propose a trial rather than a permanent change immediately. The kitchen could record sales and leftovers for a month. If the new option sells well without increasing waste, that would provide evidence for expanding it or adjusting the portion sizes later.
Sophie

Let us include a simple feedback form and accurate ingredient labels in the trial. Students could comment on taste, value and portion size. We seem to agree that affordable variety is the goal, but it should be introduced gradually and checked against actual demand.

Aisha asks for varied, affordable plant-based meals.
Tom warns that adding dishes without demand data could increase waste.
Sophie emphasises ingredient information and one rotating affordable option.
They support a month-long trial using sales, leftovers and student feedback to guide changes.

title: Making lecture recordings useful
narration: Three students are discussing how to make lecture recordings more useful for students.
turns: Ethan

I find lecture recordings very helpful because I can revisit difficult explanations and pause to check my notes. They are also useful if someone misses class for a legitimate reason. I think every lecture should be recorded and made available soon after the class finishes.
Nina

I use them too, but I sometimes postpone watching because I know the recording will be there. Then several lectures pile up before a test. Recordings are useful resources, but simply providing them does not mean students will use them effectively or keep up with the course.
Luis

Perhaps the course could provide short guides alongside each recording. Time markers for key topics would make revision easier, and a few practice questions could encourage students to check their understanding. Captions are important as well, but they should be checked because technical terms are sometimes transcribed incorrectly.
Ethan

Those additions would definitely help. I still think recordings should remain available for revision rather than disappear after a few days. Some topics make more sense later in the semester. We should encourage attendance without removing a resource that students use in different ways.
Nina

I agree about keeping access. My concern is study habits, not restricting recordings. A weekly reminder and a short self-check could help me stay on schedule. It would also be useful if teachers explained when to review a short section instead of replaying an entire lecture.
Luis

So we could recommend continued access, accurate captions, topic markers and optional self-checks. Live classes still offer questions and discussion, while recordings support review. The two should complement each other, with some guidance to help students avoid leaving all their viewing until the last minute.

title: Planning a community volunteering day
narration: Three students are planning a volunteering day at a community garden.
turns: Grace

For our student society’s volunteering day, I suggest helping at the community garden. We could do something practical outdoors and meet local residents. A full Saturday would allow us to finish a useful amount of work rather than spend most of a short visit getting organised.
Sam

I like the garden idea, but a full day may exclude students who have weekend jobs or caring responsibilities. We also should not assume that everyone can do heavy outdoor work. I would prefer flexible shifts and a choice of activities so more people can take part.
Priya

Before planning the timetable, we should ask the garden organisers what help they actually need. They may need seed sorting, signs or publicity as well as planting. A project is more useful when it supports the community’s priorities rather than just offering us an enjoyable day out.
Grace

That is a good reminder. I can contact the coordinator and ask about suitable jobs and the number of volunteers they can manage. Perhaps we could offer a morning and an afternoon shift, with some lighter tasks available under cover if the weather is poor.
Sam

Two shifts would work better for me. We should also explain transport options and any equipment people need. Students could choose activities when signing up, but we should avoid promising a particular task until the coordinator confirms that it is useful and safe.
Priya

Exactly. Once the coordinator responds, we can publish an accessible plan and arrange a short briefing. Afterwards, we should ask the garden whether our contribution was helpful. We agree on volunteering there, provided the event is flexible, well organised and shaped by the garden’s needs.

title: Tackling a college essay
narration: Three students are discussing how to tackle the challenge of writing a college essay.
turns: Speaker 1

Guys, I'm really struggling with this essay. It's so much more difficult than high school, and I have no idea where to start. It's just overwhelming. I keep rereading the prompt, but I'm still not sure if I'm interpreting it correctly.
Speaker 2

Hey, don't worry too much about it. The first thing you should do is to make sure you understand the question. Trying to write without a clear idea of what you're supposed to be discussing will just make things harder. Maybe try breaking the prompt down into smaller parts or even talk to your professor after class to clarify what they're looking for.
Speaker 3

Yeah. You don't need to start by writing the summary or introduction. Just start with the main content first. Get all your ideas down, and then you can organize them into a logical order later. I always do a brain dump first just writing everything I know or think about the topic without worrying about structure.
Speaker 2

That's true. Once you have your main points, you can write a draft and then go back and revise. You might find it easier to write the summary once you've done that. And don't forget, we're here to help, too. We can proofread your draft and give you some feedback. If you want, we could even set up a study session this weekend to go over your outline together.
Speaker 1
That sounds like a good plan. I feel much better about this now. I think I'll try the brain dump method tonight and then maybe share my rough points with you tomorrow.
Speaker 3
The writing center on campus is also a great resource. They can help you brainstorm ideas and even review your essay before you submit it.
Speaker 2

Exactly, don't hesitate to use the resources available to you. And take breaks too when you find yourself stuck. Sometimes stepping away for a bit can help clear your mind and give you a fresh perspective. I always set a timer like 45 minutes of writing, then a 10-minute break. It keeps me from burning out.
Speaker 1

Yeah, you guys make a lot of sense. I'll start by understanding the question and then move on from there. And I'll definitely use the writing center's help, too. Thank you so much! I was so stressed earlier, but now I actually have a clear starting point.
Speaker 3

You're welcome! Just remember to take it one step at a time. Writing an essay doesn't have to be a huge, insurmountable task. You're capable of breaking it down and conquering it, piece by piece. And honestly, your first draft doesn't have to be perfect just getting something on paper is already progress.
Speaker 2
Exactly, remember we're only a call away. We all struggle at times, but that's how we learn and grow. You've got this!

name: Summarise Group Discussion
instruction: Listen to three speakers. Summarise the topic, each person’s contribution, and how their views relate to one another.
title: AI tools for academic assignments
narration: Three students are debating over the pros and cons of using AI tools for academic assignments, gathered at a cozy corner table in the library lounge.
turns: Speaker 1

I have serious concerns about relying on AI for academic work. Last week, I reviewed a peer's paper that was clearly AI-generated - it sounded polished but completely lacked original thought. What's the point of education if we're not developing our own thinking abilities?
Speaker 2

I completely agree. The bigger issue is academic integrity. My professor just announced that any detected AI-generated content will result in automatic failure. It's becoming impossible to trust what's authentic anymore. Remember how we used to spend hours in the library actually engaging with sources? That struggle is where real learning happens.
Speaker 3

I understand your concerns, but I think you're overlooking the positive aspects. AI tools have been incredibly helpful for overcoming writer's block and organizing my thoughts. The outlining feature alone has saved me hours of frustration. It's not about replacing thinking - it's about enhancing it.
Speaker 1

But that's exactly the problem! When we rely on AI for organization and structure, we're missing out on developing those crucial skills ourselves. I've noticed my analytical abilities have declined since I started using these tools last semester.
Speaker 2

And what about the classroom experience? If everyone comes to class with AI-polished contributions, how do we have genuine discussions? The imperfections and hesitations in our conversations are where the most interesting insights often emerge.
Speaker 3

I see your points, but consider the accessibility benefits. For students with learning differences or those struggling with academic writing, AI tools provide crucial support that might not otherwise be available. It's not about perfect papers - it's about giving everyone a fair chance to express their ideas. These tools can help bridge gaps for neuro diverse students or those writing in a second language, allowing their ideas to be heard more clearly.
Speaker 1

I appreciate that perspective, but I worry we're creating a dependency. What happens when these tools are no longer available? Will we still know how to think for ourselves? We need to ensure we're not sacrificing fundamental skills for short-term convenience, as true intellectual development comes from working through challenges independently.
Speaker 2

That's my concern too. The value of education isn't just in the final product - it's in the struggle to get there. If we shortcut that process with AI, we're missing the most important part of learning.
Speaker 3
I guess we'll have to agree to disagree. I still believe that when used responsibly, AI can be a valuable tool rather than a threat to genuine learning. The key is finding the right balance.

Speaker 1 worries that polished AI work lacks original thought and that relying on AI weakens analytical and organisational skills.
Speaker 1 also warns about dependency and sacrificing independent intellectual development for convenience.
Speaker 2 raises academic integrity, an announced automatic-failure policy and the loss of authentic classroom discussion.
Speaker 2 believes engaging with sources and struggling through the learning process matter more than the final product alone.
Speaker 3 values AI for overcoming writer’s block, organising thoughts and supporting students with learning differences or a second language.
They remain divided: Speaker 3 advocates responsible, balanced use rather than agreeing to reject AI.

In contrast, the third speaker finds AI useful for overcoming writer’s block and organising ideas, and highlights its accessibility benefits for students with learning differences or language barriers. title: Campus part-time jobs
narration: Three students are debating the pros and cons of campus part-time jobs, gathered at a corner table in the student lounge, the air filled with the faint smell of coffee and the rustle of textbook pages.
turns: Speaker 1

I think working part-time on campus is a total waste of energy. Last month I took a job at the library desk, and between shelving books and scanning IDs, I barely had any mental capacity left for my coursework. I ended up dozing off during my morning lectures twice last week.
Speaker 2

Actually, I find my part-time job at the academic office really helpful. It forces me to manage my time better. Speaker 3

Speaker 1

Exactly! And let's be honest most of these jobs don't even relate to our future careers. I'd rather join a student club or work on a project that actually builds my resume. Stuffing envelopes or swiping cards isn't going to help me get into grad school.
Speaker 2

Speaker 1

instruction: Listen to three speakers. Summarise the topic, each person’s contribution, and how their views relate to one another.
title: On-campus and off-campus housing
narration: Three students are talking about their living experiences in on-campus dorms and off-campus housing.
turns: Speaker 1

I live in a house off campus with my friends. It's quite far from the school, but I am lucky because I live close to bus stops and it is very convenient. Also, our landlord is nice and takes care of things like cleaning and other problems around the house.
Speaker 2

I live in the school dormitory, which is very convenient, and there are places where I can study. Actually, I'd be quite happy to share a house with friends off campus, but the rent is too expensive. Also, I don't want to get up early, and the dormitory is very close to the teaching buildings.
Speaker 3

I also live in the school dormitory. If anything in the dorm breaks, it gets repaired soon, so students don't have to bother with it. Some friends living outside have problems with water and have to wait for a long time to have it fixed.
Speaker 1

That's honestly a huge advantage of living on campus. Even though our landlord is responsible and helpful, off-campus maintenance is really slow in general. We once had a water leakage issue and waited nearly a week for someone to fix it, which was really troublesome.
Speaker 2

While dorm life has plenty of benefits, it definitely comes with some annoying downsides as well. The fire alarm in our dormitory building often goes off in the middle of the night. Whenever the alarm goes off, we have to leave the building and wait until it has been checked. I'm fed up with being forced to get out of bed and evacuate outside because of fire alarms on cold winter nights.
Speaker 3

I totally agree with your opinion. I've experienced two fire alarms in the dorm, and both times they were caused by someone using a toaster illegally in the building. Can't they find the people who are cooking illegally and deal with them more quickly? Still, I think the system is quite safe, so I accept this accommodation plan.
Speaker 1

I had no idea dorm life had such annoying safety issues. Living off-campus definitely gives us more private space and flexible schedules. We can cook freely in our own kitchen without violating any campus rules, and we never suffer from sudden fire alarms at night.
Speaker 2

That sounds really relaxing, but off-campus accommodation still has obvious drawbacks. Apart from the high rent and slow maintenance, you also have to spend plenty of time on daily housework and commuting every single day.
Speaker 3

Exactly. Every living option has its own pros and cons. On-campus dorms are affordable, safe and time-saving, while off-campus houses provide more freedom and privacy. It all depends on personal study habits and lifestyle choices.

instruction: Listen to three speakers. Summarise the topic, each person’s contribution, and how their views relate to one another.
title: Choosing courses for next semester
narration: three students are discussing which course to take next semester.
turns: Speaker 1

So, have you guys checked out the course list for next semester? I skimmed through it, and I think we should pick something that's actually helpful for our major to make learning more meaningful. I'm considering research or design-survey courses. For me, high grades are not everything. As long as a course brings personal benefits and supports our future careers, that is good enough.
Speaker 2

Absolutely! I was thinking the exact same thing. There is no value in choosing an easy-high-grade course with no practical relevance. We ought to select subjects that build real-world practical skills. Curiosity will drive us to explore deeper and bring long-term rewards. I am interested in the business course, but it involves statistics, and I am not confident about my data-handling ability.
Speaker 3

Honestly, I believe personal interest should be the top priority, even if the subject is not tightly linked to our major. As a business student, I am really attracted by languages and cross-cultural content. That is why I plan to sign up for Spanish next semester. I hold the view that genuine interest helps us stay focused and pass assessments, so Spanish is my final pick.
Speaker 1

I agree interest plays an important role. Still, purely interesting courses with no major-related value can feel like a waste of time. We need to think about input-output efficiency and future job-hunting advantages. Meanwhile, course difficulty cannot be ignored; being able to pass the final exam should be a realistic goal for us.
Speaker 2

I actually disagree that Spanish has no practical value for business majors. Language skills are great assets in today's global marketplace. Whether you negotiate with overseas clients, cooperate in multicultural teams, or travel for business work, foreign-language communication brings us obvious competitive edges.
Speaker 3

To be honest, I did not weigh those career-related advantages too carefully when I made my choice. My decision mainly comes from my real passion for Spanish culture and the language itself. When you are truly fascinated by a subject, you naturally pay more attention and devote more energy to your studies. And even if the coursework gets difficult, this inner motivation can help you get through and pass.
Speaker 1

That makes sense. So there is not just one single correct way to choose courses. We have to balance practical career benefits, personal interest and the difficulty of each subject before we make our final decisions.
Speaker 2
Right. Everyone's priorities are different. Some people focus more on career preparation, while others value personal interest more. There is no one-size-fits-all answer for course selection.
Speaker 3
Exactly. The most important thing is that we are clear about our own goals, no matter which subject we end up enrolling in.

name: Summarise Group Discussion
instruction: Listen to three speakers. Summarise the topic, each person’s contribution, and how their views relate to one another.
title: AI as a proofreading tool
narration: three students are discussing using artificial intelligence as a proofreading tool.
turns: Speaker 1

Hey guys, have you ever thought about using AI for proofreading? I just got feedback on my essay from my tutor, and she said I need to proofread it. AI can check grammar for me and provide me some ideas, but I don't know if I should use AI tools because I don't want to be suspected of plagiarism.
Speaker 2

There is indeed a significant risk of being accused of plagiarism if you use AI. Many universities are now implementing strict policies about AI-generated content. If the AI suggests substantial changes to your sentence structures or replaces too many of your original words, the final work might not truly be yours anymore.
Speaker 3

Well, I don't mind using AI as long as it is for educational purposes and is used responsibly. AI can be used because students often use some computer software to check grammar, and are supposed to use others' words to improve their own vocabulary when learning linguistic expressions. In the past, we used dictionaries to check grammar, and it's really no different from using AI.
Speaker 1

Well, I get your point. I think the line when it comes to using AI for proofreading can get really blurry. I definitely don't want to be suspected of plagiarism, so is there another way I can improve my assignments next time without using AI?
Speaker 2

I'm not sure. I still think this needs to be considered carefully. For example, when Word marks mistakes with red and green underlines, is that considered AI-assisted proofreading? Different institutions and even different professors may have different standards for what counts as acceptable AI use. I'd be especially careful with major assignments or final papers.
Speaker 3

Actually, I've already been using AI on my tablet for proofreading for a while now. But, I still get asked by my teacher to do another proofread myself. I think the key thing is, you won't get any new ideas from AI. AI will only make your existing ideas clearer and more correct. It's really just an advanced tool that helps polish your work, not something that creates content for you. The fundamental thinking and ideas still need to come from you.
Speaker 1

Okay, I see. Thanks. I think I'll go back and ask for advice from my tutor about it first. I really don't want to be accused of plagiarism, especially since I'm not clear on where the line is drawn. It's better to be safe and get proper guidance rather than risk any academic consequences.
Speaker 2

That makes total sense. Since acceptance standards vary widely among teachers and universities, relying on your own judgment can be risky. It is wise to get clear instructions directly from your tutor.
Speaker 3
I agree. No matter whether you end up using AI tools or not, your own original ideas should always stay at the core of your writing.

Speaker 3 supports responsible educational proofreading to polish the student’s own ideas rather than generate content, and still proofreads personally.
Speaker 1 decides to ask the tutor for guidance, and the others support clear instructions and keeping original thinking central.

Because the boundary is unclear, the first speaker decides to ask the tutor for advice. The others support this approach and agree that original ideas should remain central to the writing.

name: Summarise Group Discussion
instruction: Listen to three speakers. Summarise the topic, each person’s contribution, and how their views relate to one another.
title: Making the university more eco-friendly
narration: Three students are discussing how to make their university more eco-friendly.
turns: Speaker 1

Hey fellas, I think there is still room for improvement when it comes to making our campus more eco-friendly. The staff should install recycling stations on key spots around the university, making it convenient for us to recycle plastic bottles, which can reduce landfill waste.
Speaker 2

Actually, we should reduce waste from the source, namely, reduce the amount of waste produced by us instead of having more bins. Just the campus cafe alone uses hundreds of paper cups every day. People should use fewer single-use coffee cups at the cafe and bring their own reusable cups.
Speaker 3

You are right. It is good for the cafeteria to use recycled paper, but they give out too many napkins at one time. Also, some packaging is too excessive, such as five layers of packaging for an apple.
Speaker 1
Yes, and students can also play a role here. We should take only what we actually need and avoid wasting food, paper, and other resources, by which we would also save money in the long run.
Speaker 3

If students bring their own bottles and cups, the university could reduce the amount of waste while students could develop more environmentally friendly habits. Another thing is more sustainable transportation. The university should build better bike paths, and provide more bike parking spaces, in order to encourage students to ride bikes with dual benefits, which is eco-friendly and great for their physical health.
Speaker 2
For students rushing between lectures, bicycles can cut their travel time. But there would be limited impact because few students own bikes. The university should establish a shared bicycle station.
Speaker 3
That sounds practical because students would not need to buy or maintain their own bicycles. They could simply rent a bike when they need one and return it after class.
Speaker 1

The university should also encourage carpooling, like having cheap parking to reward carpooling students or even free parking. It can also reduce the number of cars on campus and lower traffic congestion, especially during busy hours in the morning and afternoon.
Speaker 2

Yes, carpooling allows students to get together. Anyway, better public transport should also be considered, like buses or trains. If public transport is more convenient and reliable, students may be less dependent on private cars. This could make a bigger difference in the long term.
Speaker 1

We are a part of this green community, and should join in the eco-friendly movement. There are a lot of things to do, but we should start from small ones by ourselves, like bringing our own cups to the cafeteria, and carpooling.

title: Standards and discretion
instructions: Listen and select the words in the transcript that differ from the audio. Select a word again to remove it.
audioText: Administrative standards are often defended as a means of insulating decisions from personal preference. Their legitimacy, however, remains contingent on the purposes they serve and the circumstances in which they are applied. A rule may constrain discretion without eliminating the judgement required to interpret an unusual case. Treating every classification as provisional does not entail abandoning consistency; it acknowledges that categories can obscure distinctions relevant to a defensible decision. The crucial question is whether departures from routine are authorised through reasons that others can examine. Where decisions are reversible, institutions can learn from objections without presenting every revision as an admission of incompetence. Accountability therefore depends on making interpretations contestable while preserving a coherent explanation of why comparable cases receive comparable treatment.

title: Travel's Overrated Value
text: Travel can broaden experience, but distance alone does not guarantee learning or personal growth. title: Paper Rejection
text: Rejection is common in academic publishing and can be especially discouraging for researchers at the beginning of their careers. A rejected paper is not always worthless because reviewers may identify weak evidence, unclear argument or missing literature that can be improved. Researchers should separate useful criticism from comments that are less relevant to the goals of the study. Revising carefully before sending the work to another journal can strengthen both the paper and the author’s future research practice. Persistence matters, but so does learning from feedback rather than submitting the same unchanged manuscript repeatedly.

title: Bee Hives
text: A honeybee colony functions through highly specialised roles that allow thousands of insects to behave as a coordinated system. The queen lays eggs, workers gather food and maintain the hive, and male drones have a narrower reproductive role. Worker bees perform demanding tasks throughout short lives, while new generations continually replace those that die. Communication and division of labour allow the colony to regulate food, temperature and care for developing bees. Studying a hive shows how cooperation among individuals can produce behaviour that is more complex than the actions of any single bee.
